1:
The delay is measured first. Gill reports Jarchi's explanation that the people miscounted, taking the day of the ascent as one of the forty when Moses meant forty complete days. Henry dates the outbreak to the thirty-ninth day, and observes that the forty were given them to meditate on what was delivered while some spent them contriving how to break the laws they had received. Ellicott notes the literary seam, that after seven chapters of ritual directions the writer resumes his narrative and returns from the mount to the plain, and reports the view that these three chapters are a distinct composition inserted later. Wesley finds them weary of waiting twice over, for the promised land and for Moses. Calvin allows them no excuse, calling it detestable impiety and monstrous madness that they should speak contemptuously of the man carried above the state of terrestrial life for their sakes. Henry adds a second cause, the fury of a multitude corrupted by a few who lie in wait to deceive, so that many were carried down the stream who would never have thought of it themselves.

Aaron's part is judged with care, and the judgments differ. Ellicott calls it a reasonable conjecture that he meant to prevent the idolatry, lacking courage for a direct refusal and hoping to divert them by asking a sacrifice they would be unwilling to make. Wesley reports the same view from others, that the demand was meant to crush the proposal since pride would refuse what covetousness might allow, while noting that Aaron said not a word to discountenance it. Calvin grants the subterfuge but refuses it as an excuse, asking why, if he meant no harm, he did not order the gold thrown into a chest rather than take it into his own hands. Keil and Delitzsch put it as plain succumbing: instead of opposing the proposal and raising their despondency into living faith by pointing to the deeds through which Jehovah had proved himself faithful, Aaron fell with the people. Ellicott adds that the calculation failed, not the slightest objection being made and all the people surrendering their earrings with one accord.

The word rendered graving tool is disputed. Clarke reports a long controversy, some making it a mould, others a garment, others a bag, others a graver, and supposes that a mould was made and the form finished with chisel and graver. Ellicott takes the other side outright, that the sense is he bound it in a bag, citing Gesenius and Rosenmüller, since a graving tool cannot precede a clause calling the image molten. Clarke observes the irony that ornaments granted by God's providence should be abused to the basest purpose, the people's bent to idolatry outrunning even their love of dress.

The feast is read as a mixture, not a simple apostasy. Wesley insists they did not mean to terminate their worship in the image but made it a representation of the true God, which excuses them no more than those who plead the same today. Ellicott notes that Aaron, having yielded once, was carried from one compliance to another, building the altar of rough stones and setting it directly before the image; Calvin makes him the pattern of all who will not maintain what is right but bargain and compromise, vacillating a while and at last succumbing altogether. Gill reports the Targums that Aaron saw Hur slain before him for reproving the idolatry; Keil and Delitzsch describe the feast with its offerings, its eating and drinking, its sports and antiphonal singing. Clarke explains the meal from the ritual, the burnt offerings being wholly consumed while the peace offerings became food once the blood was poured out, so they ate as idolaters do, to excess. Calvin marks their diligence in appearing at the very dawn, and asks what is to be said of our sloth if unbelievers are driven so headlong.
7:
God's own account of the sin is analysed clause by clause. Henry asks why the news was delayed, and answers that God could have told Moses at the first step and prevented it, but suffered it to come to this height for wise ends and then sent him to punish it; it is no reproach to God's holiness to suffer sin, since he knows how to restrain it and how to make it serve his glory. He takes the three charges in order: that they had corrupted themselves, sin being a self-corruption since every man is tempted when drawn aside of his own lust; that they had turned aside out of the way, a deviation from duty into a by-path; and that they had turned aside quickly, soon after the law was given and they had promised to obey it. Keil and Delitzsch make the haste an aggravation which rendered their ingratitude the more glaring, and Calvin adds that the plea put forward to colour their ungodliness is alleged last, as the climax of the sin. Ellicott notes that the imperative implies urgency, Moses being hidden by the cloud from all that passed in the plain.

The disowning word is felt by all. Ellicott glosses it exactly, thine and no longer mine, since they have broken the covenant that united us. Clarke reads it as disinheritance, the people having become abominable so that they forfeit God's protection, and turns the passage against the image-worship of his own day. Calvin makes it the sorest trial for Moses, who had thought all secure when the covenant was engraven on tables, and now hears it violated and almost annihilated. Ellicott adds that stiff-necked, afterwards so common, occurs here first and means perverse rather than obstinate, the metaphor taken from a horse stiffening his neck against the rein; Clarke suspects a sharper allusion, to the neck of the very ox they had worshipped, and Wesley glosses it as unapt to come under the yoke of the divine law.

The words let me alone are the crux, and nearly every voice reads them as invitation rather than prohibition. Clarke observes that the Omnipotent here represents himself unable to act in judgment unless his creature desist from praying, and compares Abraham pleading for Sodom. Ellicott denies it is a command to abstain from deprecation and calls it an intimation that deprecation might change God's purpose, Moses being tried by an offer which would have exalted him at the people's expense, so that his choice redounds to his honour. Wesley answers that God speaks after the manner of men who would have none intercede for those they mean to punish, so putting an honour upon prayer. Gill alone keeps it a prohibition, citing the Targum: leave off thy prayer, and cry not for them before me.

The plea is examined for its grounds. Gill observes that Moses uses his own interest in a covenant God, and that a good man is concerned for God's honour among his people's enemies. Wesley reads the appeal as taking the hint God gave, since let me alone, though it seemed to forbid intercession, really encouraged it. Calvin holds that the prayer sprang from faith although it seems to fight against the very word of God, Moses answering nay, they are thine, and grasping so firmly the principle that God's covenant cannot be made ineffective that he breaks through every obstacle with closed eyes; the patriarchs are named not as patrons whose voice might help but because the promise was lodged with them. On the repenting Gill denies that any determination of God is alterable, what changes being the outward dispensation of his providence, and Clarke that the word is spoken after the manner of men diverted from a purpose by strong reasons; Wesley draws the lesson, that God suffers himself to be prevailed with by humble believing importunity.
15:
The tables themselves are described before the descent. Henry calls it a favour that Moses was trusted with them, common stone though they were, more valuable than all the precious stones on Aaron's breastplate, and holds that God wrote the commandments without the ministry of man or angel. Clarke finds the writing on both sides unusual, since in ancient times the two sides of one substance were never written over, and reports the rabbinic supposition that the letters were cut through so as to be legible on either face. Ellicott notes that Babylonian and Assyrian tablets are so inscribed; Wesley takes the two sides to mean some commandments on one table and some on the other, folded like a book to be laid in the ark. On the workmanship Ellicott reports Rosenmüller's view that only the size and shape were prescribed, but holds the natural sense to be that God fashioned the stones himself, which was not the case with the second tables; Gill says the same. Wesley remarks that this was very probably the first writing in the world, and Calvin observes that God left the tables untouched in Moses' hands even after pronouncing sentence.

The mistaken noise is a small scene they enjoy. Henry describes the arrangement, Moses in the cloud as in the presence-chamber and Joshua waiting in the antechamber, alone for forty days and fed, it is likely, with manna, yet not weary of waiting as the people were. Ellicott adds that Joshua stayed where he was when his master was summoned into the cloud, perhaps sheltering in a cleft of the rock. Clarke finds the guess natural to a military man, who hearing a confused noise supposed the camp attacked. Ellicott presses the Hebrew, that the same verb stands in all three clauses, so it is the voice neither of those who cry for victory nor of those who cry for defeat but simply of those who cry, Moses' hearing yielding no positive result. Calvin draws the moral instead, that a shouting heard so far off shows how intemperately they raged, and that this is how the devil bewitches men, so that dissolute licentiousness passes for pious ardour.

The breaking of the tables is defended rather than excused. Wesley denies that it breaches the law of meekness to show displeasure at wickedness, since those are angry and sin not who are angry at sin only, and holds that Moses broke the tables and burnt the calf to awaken the people by these expressions of strong passion. Calvin makes the same point against the Stoics: anger is here mentioned with praise, so their paradox that all the passions are vicious must be abandoned, though men led by nature are never angry without vice. Clarke offers two accounts, distress and anguish of spirit or, more probably, an emblem that the covenant was as broken as the stones; Ellicott says righteous indignation and perhaps design, and notes that the dances Moses saw were of the kind uniformly lascivious among Oriental nations.

The destruction of the idol is described exactly and then interpreted. Keil and Delitzsch give the process, the fire calcining the wooden centre and melting the golden coating, what was left being ground to powder and strewed on the water. Clarke meets the objection that gold could not be stamped to dust, answering from Deuteronomy, and marks the contempt of making them drink their god. Gill notes that it was melted into a mass and lost its form, and Wesley draws the lesson, that to show an idol is nothing in the world he reduced it to atoms and strewed it on the water they all drank, so that the whole camp should take notice. Calvin alone hesitates: the punishment might seem cruel, infecting the very bowels of the people with the corruption of their crime and likely to drive them to despair.
21:
Aaron is called to account first. Henry says Moses begins with him as God began with Adam, because he was the principal person though not first in the transgression but drawn into it, and marks the difference in the treatment, that Aaron was reproved and not cut off like the ringleaders, since much is to be made between those who rush presumptuously into sin and those who through infirmity are surprised into it; he would have been cut off but for the intercession recorded in Deuteronomy. Gill and Ellicott ground the questioning in the trust, Ellicott asking how Aaron acquitted himself of a commission to advise, direct and control. Calvin puts it as a principle, that a man possessed of power seems to permit the evil he does not prevent, and Clarke in a line, that if Aaron had been firm this evil might have been prevented.

The excuse is heard and dismissed. Gill notes the respectful address to a younger brother who was nevertheless chief ruler. Calvin grants that the modesty of the opening is right enough but calls the excuse frivolous, Clarke that Aaron pleads the seditious spirit of the people as though obliged to accede, and Keil and Delitzsch will not allow even weakness to acquit him. The worst of it is the account of the making. Clarke calls it a silly and ridiculous subterfuge to insinuate that he only threw the metal in and the calf came out by accident, and reports that the Targum of Jonathan repeats the same excuse. Wesley says it is natural to us to transfer our guilt thus, Aaron extenuating his share as though he had only bidden them break off their gold.

One word in the next verse is disputed. Gill denies that naked can mean stripped of their earrings, since parting with those would not warrant the term, or without their armour. Clarke reports the Targum that they were stripped of the holy crown bearing the divine name, but thinks the Hebrew implies a helpless state, abandoned by God among their enemies. Ellicott notes that most modern commentators prefer licentious or unruly, but defends the received rendering, since in idolatrous orgies garments were cast aside and the person exposed, as the Egyptian monuments show; he marks too that the idol had been seized and Aaron shamed, yet the revel continued, so a crowning step had to be taken. Wesley catches the imagery, that the idolaters had set up the calf for their standard and Moses now sets up his in opposition.

The slaughter is the hardest thing in the chapter and none of them softens it. Gill places Moses in the gate as the usual place of judgment, and insists that the orders were not the effect of heat and passion but came expressly from God. Ellicott says the same, that Moses felt himself divinely commissioned, that the lives of all who had committed the idolatry were justly forfeit, and that trial was unnecessary where the offence was openly committed, since such dancing could not possibly be the worship of Jehovah. Calvin admits the command may seem cruel, the Levites being forbidden to spare brothers, friends and neighbours, but denies it excessive if we reflect how much graver it is to profane the worship of God than to injure men, and holds the slaughter a reminder that all had deserved the same. Clarke takes the three thousand for the chief transgressors, who by having other gods lost the divine protection; Wesley reads the order more narrowly, as reaching only those found abroad in the street, those retired into their tents being hoped ashamed. On the consecration Ellicott explains that a brave behaviour would win the tribe a semi-priestly character, made good when the Levites were appointed to the sanctuary in place of the firstborn; Clarke glosses the Hebrew as filling the hand to the Lord.
30:
Moses first turns back to the survivors. Henry has him tell them plainly that they have sinned a great sin, lest those spared should suppose that exemption from the capital punishment meant exemption from guilt, and draws the rule that the work of ministers is to show people their sins and the greatness of their sins, a great sin calling for great sorrow because it puts men in great danger. Calvin sees a double purpose: the judgment being terrible he consoles them lest they despair, while reminding them of the enormity of their sin so that they may come as suppliants. Gill dates the sequence from the rabbis: the tables broken on the seventeenth, the calf burnt on the eighteenth, the intercession made on the nineteenth. Wesley catches the wording of the confession, that Moses calls them not God's people but this people, this treacherous and ungrateful people; Ellicott adds that gods of gold should rather be a god of gold, the plural being one of dignity.

The broken sentence at the heart of the plea is noticed by all. Ellicott explains it as aposiopesis, some phrase such as well and good being left unspoken after the word sin, cites parallels in Daniel, Luke and Romans, and remarks that the usage is common among Orientals; he holds too that Moses rose to the height of self-abnegation St Paul afterwards reached. Wesley supplies the other half, that if the decree has gone forth Moses is content to perish with them, comparing Paul wishing himself accursed for his brethren. Clarke gives the book a concrete sense, supposing part of the forty days spent regulating the muster-roll of the tribes, so that to be blotted out is to be struck from that register.

The answer is a refusal on principle. Ellicott sets it beside Ezekiel's word that the soul which sins shall die, and argues that a mere man cannot take other men's sins upon him nor relieve them of the penalty, the worst of which is the depravation of the soul; Wesley says the same in a line, and Clarke expands it into a speech, that all God's conduct is regulated by justice and in no case shall the innocent suffer for the guilty. Calvin observes that God adapts himself here to the human mind, since hypocrites profess his name so plausibly that they are not reckoned aliens until he openly renounces them, which is why their rejection is called erasure; and he grants that God reproves the request as inconsistent with his justice. Keil and Delitzsch set the exchange out as it stands.

The close is a reprieve with a reservation. Clarke observes that the word place is not in the text and is rightly omitted, Moses never leading the people into the land but only towards it. Ellicott notes that the promise of the angel nearly repeats the original one, and Calvin takes the appointment as the sure sign of reconciliation, rejecting as a poor exposition the view that it was merely such an angel as heathen nations had. Wesley takes the opposite line, that it was a created angel of the common services of the kingdom, intimating that nothing thereafter was to be expected out of the common road of providence. On the last verse Gill and Wesley take the plaguing of some later stroke and not of the three thousand already slain, Wesley concluding that Moses obtained a mitigation but could not wholly turn away the wrath; Calvin reads it the other way, that Moses attributes to God what he had already related of the slaughter, lest any should think he had smitten them with immoderate severity. Ellicott denies that a pestilence is meant and takes it of sufferings of various kinds; Clarke reports the Jewish saying that no affliction ever befell Israel without some particle of the dust of the golden calf in it.
